title: Limits of Machine Intelligence
lines: Limits of Machine Intelligence examines what impossibility theorems do, and do not, forbid.
It distinguishes a universal decision procedure from bounded certificates for a particular operating envelope.
The book develops this distinction through the exploratory philosophy of outfinitism.
It preserves classical limits while asking where boundary detection and suspended judgment become useful.
Readers can evaluate a proposed framework without treating it as an established mathematical foundation.

title: Finite does not mean easy
lines: A finite operating domain can permit exhaustive checking while remaining computationally impractical.
Some diagonal limits still apply because their transformations use finite descriptions.
The book therefore distinguishes logical possibility from feasible verification.
Outfinitism asks what a finite agent is entitled to claim at its current frontier.
Its vocabulary is a proposal whose usefulness must be demonstrated.

title: When the frontier moves
lines: A certificate depends on assumptions about its domain, resources, precision, and operating conditions.
Moving beyond those conditions requires justification for carrying the result forward.
The book treats boundary detection, fallback, cost, and unresolved status as substantive obligations.
Existing verification techniques supply important comparisons rather than being displaced by a new name.
This makes the proposed philosophy answerable to actual assurance problems.

title: Read the qualifications
lines: Begin with the distinction between global impossibility and a particular bounded claim.
Read the mathematical examples alongside the cases where important limits remain intact.
The final research discussion asks whether the framework improves evaluation beyond existing vocabulary.
Limits of Machine Intelligence is an exploratory argument, not an established replacement for mathematics.
Read it to examine exactly what changes when a machine's operating frontier becomes explicit.
